concepts.name: Purpose of a message
concepts.summary: State in one sentence why you are writing and what you want the reader to know or do.

concepts.name: Audience awareness
concepts.summary: Explain how the reader's role, knowledge and needs shape what you include and how you say it.

concepts.name: Common workplace document types
concepts.summary: Recognise what emails, memos, reports and proposals are each used for and when each fits.

concepts.name: Clear subject lines
concepts.summary: Write a specific subject line that tells the reader the topic and any needed action.

concepts.name: Plain, concise wording
concepts.summary: Choose short, familiar words and cut filler so each sentence carries one clear point.

concepts.name: Professional tone basics
concepts.summary: Distinguish a polite, respectful, neutral workplace tone from slang, rudeness or over-casual phrasing.

concepts.name: Opening and closing conventions
concepts.summary: Use appropriate greetings and sign-offs and include a clear closing line.

misconceptions.text: Longer, more formal wording sounds more professional and is therefore better.
A subject line is optional because the reader will open the email anyway.
Every workplace message should be written the same way regardless of who reads it.

concepts.name: Lead with the main point
concepts.summary: Open a message with the conclusion, request or decision before giving supporting detail.

concepts.name: Paragraph structure
concepts.summary: Build short paragraphs that each start with a topic sentence and develop a single idea.

concepts.name: Active voice and strong verbs
concepts.summary: Rewrite passive, noun-heavy sentences so the actor and action are clear and direct.

concepts.name: Clear requests and deadlines
concepts.summary: Phrase a request so it states who should do what by when.

concepts.name: Formatting for scanning
concepts.summary: Use headings, bullets, numbered lists and white space to make content easy to scan.

concepts.name: Adjusting formality
concepts.summary: Adapt formality and warmth to the relationship and situation, such as a manager versus a client.

concepts.name: Proofreading routine
concepts.summary: Check for errors, names, attachments and facts systematically before sending.

misconceptions.text: Building up background first is more polite than stating the main point at the start.
Passive voice is always more professional and should be used in business writing.
Hinting at what you need is enough; readers will work out the request.

concepts.name: Audience analysis for design
concepts.summary: Analyse a reader's knowledge, priorities, objections and decision power to decide content, depth and order.

concepts.name: Direct versus indirect structure
concepts.summary: Choose between leading with the point or building toward it, based on expected reader reaction, especially for bad news.

concepts.name: Report structure and executive summary
concepts.summary: Organise a report into purpose, findings, analysis and recommendations with a standalone summary.

concepts.name: Evidence and recommendations
concepts.summary: Link data and findings logically to conclusions and specific recommendations.

concepts.name: Structural editing
concepts.summary: Revise a draft for order, completeness and relevance before polishing sentences.

concepts.name: Tone and emotional impact
concepts.summary: Analyse how word choice conveys attitude and rework phrasing to be reader-centred and constructive.

concepts.name: Email threads and recipients
concepts.summary: Manage recipients, threads and forwarding so the right people get the right information.

misconceptions.text: Bad news should always be stated bluntly first, whatever the reader's situation.
An executive summary is just the introduction copied shorter.
Editing means fixing grammar and wording; reorganising is rewriting, not editing.

concepts.name: Persuasive proposal design
concepts.summary: Build a proposal that frames the problem, justifies the solution, addresses costs and risks, and fits the decision-maker's criteria.

concepts.name: Writing for mixed audiences
concepts.summary: Layer a document so executives, specialists and implementers each find what they need.

concepts.name: Evaluating argument strength
concepts.summary: Judge whether claims, evidence and assumptions in a draft are sufficient and fair, and fix weak points.

concepts.name: Handling sensitive messages
concepts.summary: Judge when and how to write about complaints, refusals or conflict, and when written form is the wrong channel.

concepts.name: Data presentation in text
concepts.summary: Select and caption tables or charts and write the interpretation that makes the numbers meaningful.

concepts.name: Style consistency and templates
concepts.summary: Apply and adapt organisational style guides and templates while keeping content clear.

concepts.name: Peer review and feedback
concepts.summary: Give prioritised, actionable feedback on a colleague's writing and judge feedback you receive.

misconceptions.text: A strong proposal mainly lists the features and credentials of the writer's own solution.
Charts and tables speak for themselves and need no written interpretation.
Written messages are always the best way to handle a sensitive issue because they create a record.

concepts.name: Communication strategy design
concepts.summary: Design a coordinated set of written communications that sequences messages, channels and timing to achieve organisational goals.

concepts.name: Cross-cultural writing judgement
concepts.summary: Evaluate how directness, hierarchy, idiom and politeness norms affect understanding across cultures and adapt accordingly.

concepts.name: Creating writing standards
concepts.summary: Create guidelines, templates and review processes that raise writing quality across a team or organisation.

concepts.name: Risk, legal and ethical review
concepts.summary: Evaluate written communications for legal exposure, confidentiality, bias and misleading framing.

concepts.name: Coaching writers
concepts.summary: Develop others' writing by diagnosing patterns and designing targeted practice and feedback.

concepts.name: Voice and narrative in leadership
concepts.summary: Craft messages that use narrative and a consistent voice to build trust and motivate change.

concepts.name: Measuring communication effectiveness
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether writing achieved its goals using response, action and comprehension evidence and refine accordingly.

misconceptions.text: One well-written message is enough to drive organisational change.
Plain, direct English works equally well in every culture.
A strict style guide alone guarantees good writing across a team.
